title: Causal Fingerprints Reveal Hidden Mechanisms in Partially-Observed Dynamical Systems

paper.title: Causal Fingerprints Reveal Hidden Mechanisms in Partially-Observed Dynamical Systems
paper.abstract: Abstract In partially-observed dynamical systems, distinct hidden mechanisms can produce similar observable summary statistics while explaining individual events differently. Matching statistics therefore does not guarantee matching mechanisms. We introduce causal fingerprints: realization-dependent patterns that track how information about a hidden state is revealed through subsequent evolution. Within a prescribed dynamical model, we compare the filtering posterior, based on observations up to a given time, with the smoothing posterior, obtained after adding an expanding window of future observations. We quantify this retrospective information gain using Kullback-Leibler divergence and track its evolution as the future window of observational data expands. The fingerprint reveals both the strength and temporal reach of hidden influence, which can vary across events and their stages. Because the observed trajectory is held fixed while hidden-state inference depends on the candidate model, fingerprints reveal how competing dynamical mechanisms explain the same observations even when selected statistics agree. In linear Gaussian systems, we derive a characteristic fingerprint timescale for the temporal reach of hidden influence. Calibrated surrogates matching the observable mean, variance, and decorrelation time can still produce distinct fingerprints when feedback memory, hidden-noise memory, or hidden forcing timescales are misrepresented. Nonlinear examples reveal mechanism-dependent signatures for extreme bursts, oscillatory variability, and regime switching, including multiplicative instability versus additive forcing, deterministic nonlinear feedback versus state-dependent multiplicative noise, and intrinsic bistability versus hidden double-well forcing. Causal fingerprints therefore provide a time- and event-resolved diagnostic for asking not only whether a model reproduces observed statistics, but how its hidden dynamics explain individual events.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Complex dynamical systems arise throughout science and engineering, including geophysical dynamics [ 1 ] , turbulence [ 2 ] , neuroscience [ 3 ] , epidemiology [ 4 ] , and financial markets [ 5 ] . A defining feature of many such systems is that they are partially observed: in practice, the observed variables represent only a subset of the full dynamical state, while many relevant variables remain hidden or unresolved due to limited observations, coarse-grained modeling, or intrinsic spatiotemporal multiscale structures [ 6 ] . These hidden variables often represent slow environmental drivers, unresolved sub-grid or small-scale processes [ 2 ] , or latent regulatory mechanisms [ 3 ] . A central challenge in studying partially-observed systems is that different hidden mechanisms can produce very similar observable statistics, such as probability distributions, autocorrelations, or energy spectra [ 7 , 8 ] . As a result, model identification based solely on observable statistics can admit different explanations for the underlying latent dynamics [ 9 ] . Understanding the causal influence that hidden variables have on the observables’ evolution is therefore essential, providing insight into the mechanisms that drive observable variability and shape phenomena such as extreme events [ 10 ] , oscillatory variability [ 11 ] , and regime transitions [ 12 ] . In dynamical systems, such influence can vary substantially along a trajectory and across different stages of an event, making time-local and event-resolved diagnosis particularly important. Existing causal inference frameworks have been successfully applied to a wide range of dynamical systems. Methods such as Granger causality [ 13 ] , transfer entropy [ 14 ] , and graphical-model-based approaches [ 15 ] are particularly useful for identifying statistical or predictive relationships among observed, or reliably reconstructed, variables. However, their considered setting poses two significant difficulties. First, some of the variables responsible for the observed evolution are themselves hidden. Second, their influence may change substantially along a trajectory, so relationships inferred from long records can miss mechanisms that become important only during a particular event or stage of an event. Our interest is therefore not only in whether a causal relationship exists on average, but in how hidden influence unfolds during an individual realization. A complementary line of work uses dynamical structures more explicitly. Information-flow formulations [ 16 ] , perturbation experiments [ 17 ] , and response-theory approaches [ 18 ] , including fluctuation-dissipation methods, use the governing dynamics to characterize directional entropy transfer, sensitivity, or response to perturbations. The question considered here is different: an observed trajectory is given while important causal variables remain hidden, with candidate models providing competing explanations for the latent dynamics behind that trajectory. This motivates the concept of causal fingerprints for partially-observed dynamical systems. Distinct latent mechanisms can produce similar observable statistics, making them difficult to distinguish using probability distributions, long-time correlations, or related diagnostics [ 19 , 7 ] . Yet they need not explain an individual trajectory in the same way. Hidden influence may become important at different stages of an event or remain relevant over different future horizons. We refer to these realization-dependent temporal patterns of hidden-to-observed influence as causal fingerprints. Building on assimilative causal inference and related work on causal influence ranges [ 10 , 20 ] , we use these realization-dependent fingerprints to diagnose competing dynamical mechanisms. Fingerprints computed under different candidate models can be compared along the same observed trajectory, revealing differences in the hidden dynamical explanations assigned to the observations. To quantify these patterns, we adopt a Bayesian inverse-problem perspective of causality [ 10 ] . When a hidden state affects the subsequent observed evolution, later observations can sharpen the inference of that earlier state. Using data assimilation [ 21 , 22 ] , we compare the filtering posterior based on observations up to the current time with the smoothing posterior obtained after incorporating an expanding window of future observations [ 23 ] . Extending this future window tracks how far information about the hidden state persists in the subsequent observations. Repeating the comparison along the trajectory shows how this pattern changes across events and during their various stages of onset, development, peak, and decay. The diagnostic is therefore observation-conditioned but model-informed: the observed trajectory is fixed, while hidden-state inference depends on the candidate dynamical model. Fingerprints computed from the same observations can consequently reveal how different hidden mechanisms explain the same observed evolution. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 presents the mathematical formulation, definition, and interpretation of causal fingerprints. Section 3 develops the analyses and mechanism tests for linear Gaussian systems. Section 4 examines nonlinear dynamical systems involving extreme events, oscillatory variability, and regime switching. Section 5 summarizes the numerical findings and discusses future directions. Additional derivations and exposition can be found in the Appendix.

sections.heading: 2 Causal Fingerprints in Partially-Observed Systems
sections.text: This section develops the causal-fingerprint framework for partially-observed dynamical systems. The central idea is to compare what can be inferred about a hidden state from observations available up to a given time with what can be inferred about the same state after subsequent observations are added. If that hidden state affects the later observed evolution, those later observations should carry information about it.

sections.heading: 2.1 Partially-observed dynamical systems
sections.text: We consider dynamical systems in which only a subset of the state variables is observed, while the remaining variables are hidden. sections.heading: 2.2 Definition of the causal fingerprint
sections.text: Consider a prescribed dynamical model of the form ( 1 ) (hereafter called the inference model), which we use to infer the hidden state from an observed trajectory. At state time t t , the filtering distribution p ⁡ ( 𝐘 t ∣ 𝐗 [ 0 , t ] ) p(\mathbf{Y}_{t}\mid\mathbf{X}_{[0,t]}) describes what can be inferred about 𝐘 t \mathbf{Y}_{t} from the observations available up to that time, 𝐗 [ 0 , t ] = { 𝐗 s : 0 ≤ s ≤ t } \mathbf{X}_{[0,t]}=\{\mathbf{X}_{s}:0\leq s\leq t\} . After observations over a future window ( t , t + τ ] (t,t+\tau] are added, the corresponding smoothing distribution becomes p ⁡ ( 𝐘 t ∣ 𝐗 [ 0 , t + τ ] ) p(\mathbf{Y}_{t}\mid\mathbf{X}_{[0,t+\tau]}) . The two conditional distributions concern the same hidden state. Their difference comes only from the information contained in the subsequent observed evolution. This filter-smoother comparison gives the inverse-problem interpretation of hidden causal influence used here. If 𝐘 t \mathbf{Y}_{t} affects the subsequent evolution of 𝐗 \mathbf{X} under the prescribed dynamics, then the consequences of that influence can leave information in the later observations 𝐗 [ 0 , t + τ ] \mathbf{X}_{[0,t+\tau]} . Those observations can therefore revise the inference of the earlier hidden state. The causal interpretation comes from this temporal relation and the dynamical model; the divergence introduced below quantifies the resulting information gain. For a realized observed trajectory 𝐗 \mathbf{X} , we define the causal fingerprint at state time t t and future-window length τ \tau as the smoother-to-filter Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence [ 26 , 27 ] : Causal Fingerprint: ℐ ( t , τ ) := D KL ( p ( 𝐘 t ∣ 𝐗 [ 0 , t + τ ] ) ∥ p ( 𝐘 t ∣ 𝐗 [ 0 , t ] ) ) . \mbox{Causal Fingerprint:}\qquad\mathcal{I}(t,\tau):=D_{\mathrm{KL}}\left(p(\mathbf{Y}_{t}\mid\mathbf{X}_{[0,t+\tau]})\|p(\mathbf{Y}_{t}\mid\mathbf{X}_{[0,t]})\right). D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|q):=\int p(\mathbf{y})\log\frac{p(\mathbf{y})}{q(\mathbf{y})}\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{y}. As the future window length τ \tau expands, the fingerprint records how long subsequent observations continue to refine the inference of 𝐘 t \mathbf{Y}_{t} . It therefore probes the temporal reach of the model-implied influence of the hidden state on the observed evolution [ 20 ] . The dependence on t t makes this diagnostic trajectory-dependent: the instantaneous strength and temporal reach of hidden influence can change from one event to another and across different stages of the same event.

(4) Therefore, the average causal fingerprint recovers the same conditional-information principle underlying causation entropy: a cause is informative when its knowledge reduces the uncertainty about a subsequent effect. In addition, by symmetry of the conditional mutual information, the averaged fingerprint in ( 4 ) equals H ⁡ ( 𝐘 t ∣ 𝐗 [ 0 , t ] ) − H ⁡ ( 𝐘 t ∣ 𝐗 [ 0 , t + τ ] ) H(\mathbf{Y}_{t}\mid\mathbf{X}_{[0,t]})-H(\mathbf{Y}_{t}\mid\mathbf{X}_{[0,t+\tau]}) , expressing how subsequent observations reduce uncertainty about their earlier hidden cause. For an individual observed trajectory, the causal fingerprint provides a pathwise counterpart of this inverse-problem interpretation through Bayesian data assimilation. For a fixed state time t t , varying the future-window length τ \tau shows how far the causal influence assigned to the hidden state 𝐘 t \mathbf{Y}_{t} remains visible in the subsequent observations 𝐗 [ 0 , t + τ ] \mathbf{X}_{[0,t+\tau]} . Moving the state time along a trajectory 𝐗 \mathbf{X} shows how this influence changes as an event develops. The observed trajectory itself is held fixed, but the inferred hidden state and its fingerprint depend on the candidate model. Comparing fingerprints obtained from the same observations under different models therefore reveals how competing hidden mechanisms explain the same observed evolution.

sections.heading: 3 Mechanism Discrimination in Linear Gaussian Partially-Observed Systems
sections.text: The framework developed in Section 2 leaves open whether the temporal structure of the causal fingerprint can discriminate misrepresented hidden mechanisms or omitted latent components. In this section, we study this question in linear Gaussian systems, where the filtering and smoothing distributions, as well as the fingerprint itself, can be computed analytically in closed form. In this setting, we analyze the memory effects in the evolution of the observed variable and derive a characteristic timescale for the temporal reach of hidden causal influence. We perform two tests in this section. In each test, a perfect model serves as the generator that produces a fixed reference trajectory of X X under specific latent dynamical mechanisms. The perfect and surrogate models then serve as inference models for computing fingerprints along this same realized trajectory. The corresponding surrogate models omit or suppress mechanisms present in the perfect model but are nevertheless calibrated to reproduce the same selected observable statistics. We then investigate whether causal fingerprints can reveal the mechanistic differences between the perfect and surrogate models despite this statistical agreement in the observable state space. Test I considers a perfect model with both feedback-induced state memory and hidden-noise memory. Its two surrogates respectively remove the feedback-induced state memory and strongly suppress the hidden-noise memory. Test II considers a perfect model with slow and fast hidden forcing components and a lower-dimensional surrogate with just a single hidden forcing component.

sections.heading: 3.3 Test I: feedback-induced state memory versus hidden-noise memory

sections.heading: 3.4 Test II: one-timescale versus two-timescale hidden forcing
sections.text: In Test II we investigate whether causal fingerprints can discriminate the omission of a hidden forcing timescale in a lower-dimensional reduced-order model. The perfect model is temporally multiscale and drives X t X_{t} with slow and fast hidden forcing components, whereas the reduced model uses a single hidden forcing component. Similar to Test I, both the perfect and reduced models are calibrated to produce the same selected stationary statistics (the mean, variance V X V_{X} , and decorrelation time 𝒯 X \mathcal{T}_{X} ) of X X , while their fingerprints are computed from the same reference trajectory of X X , generated by the perfect model. Under the perfect model, the joint causal fingerprint of the slow-fast latent scales characterizes the joint causal influence of the two hidden forcing components on X X , while the marginal causal fingerprints characterize the causal influence of each component on X X . Test II examines whether the perfect-model fingerprint reveals distinct temporal patterns associated with the slow and fast hidden forcing components and whether the reduced-model fingerprint preserves this multiscale structure.

sections.heading: 4 Event-Level Causal Diagnostics for Nonlinear Mechanisms
sections.text: In Section 3 , we studied how causal fingerprints respond when reduced models omit or suppress hidden mechanisms even after the surrogate models are calibrated to match the same selected observable summary statistics. We now extend this diagnostic approach to nonlinear examples, examining how competing model mechanisms assign hidden influence during different stages of the same observed event. Models with different latent dynamical mechanisms can produce closely matched conventional summary statistics and similar classes of events, yet provide different mechanistic explanations for the same observed trajectory [ 41 , 42 ] . In each case study, we consider two models that represent different mechanistic interpretations for the same type of observed event. The model parameters are chosen so that the two models produce closely matched values of selected observable statistics. With these parameters fixed, we generate one reference trajectory from each model containing the event of interest. Then, for each reference trajectory, both models are used as inference models: under this setup, the case study is self-consistent when the inference model is the generating model for the reference trajectory and mechanism-mismatched when it is the other model. We consider three nonlinear examples: multiplicative instability versus additive hidden forcing as alternative mechanisms for intermittent extreme events; deterministic nonlinear feedback versus state-dependent stochastic forcing for oscillatory variability; and deterministic bistability versus hidden double-well forcing for regime switching and tipping.

sections.heading: 4.1 Extreme events: multiplicative instability versus additive forcing
sections.text: Intermittent extreme events can arise when a system temporarily enters an unstable regime or experiences strong additive forcing [ 43 , 44 ] . sections.heading: 4.2 Oscillatory variability: nonlinear feedback versus state-dependent stochastic forcing
sections.text: Oscillatory variability can be strongly asymmetric between its positive and negative phases. Similar observable asymmetry can arise from different latent dynamical mechanisms, including nonlinear deterministic feedback and stochastic forcing whose amplitude depends on the system state. These mechanisms may reproduce comparable low-order statistics while assigning different roles to hidden variables during individual events. They therefore provide a useful test of whether causal fingerprints can separate competing explanations of oscillatory behavior. As a concrete case study, we consider the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) [ 45 , 46 ] , a coupled ocean-atmosphere mode of variability in the tropical Pacific with characteristic periods of roughly 3 3 – 7 7 years [ 11 ] . Its warm phase, El Niño, and cold phase, La Niña, are associated with opposite sea-surface-temperature (SST) anomalies and changes in upper-ocean heat content. The slow recharge and discharge of equatorial heat content helps organize transitions between these phases [ 47 ] . ENSO also exhibits pronounced warm-cold asymmetry, including positive SST skewness in the eastern equatorial Pacific, while stochastic atmospheric forcing can modify the development and transition of individual events [ 11 ] . The recharge oscillator (RO) provides a low-dimensional framework for representing these coupled SST and upper-ocean dynamics [ 48 , 11 ] . Extensions of the RO model can reproduce ENSO asymmetry through different mechanisms, including nonlinear deterministic feedbacks and state-dependent stochastic forcing. We use these two alternatives to examine whether causal fingerprints reveal how competing mechanisms assign hidden influence during the same type of oscillatory event. Simple RO models typically use an SST anomaly T t T_{t} and an upper-ocean heat-content or thermocline-depth anomaly h t h_{t} . The precise definitions of these variables vary across RO formulations [ 11 ] . Here, T t T_{t} is treated as the observed variable, while h t h_{t} is a hidden recharge variable expressed as a thermocline-depth anomaly. The variables T t T_{t} and h t h_{t} are measured in kelvin and meters, respectively, and time is measured in years. The first model represents nonlinear deterministic feedback, combining linear coupling between T t T_{t} and h t h_{t} with quadratic and cubic SST-anomaly feedback terms: d ​ T t \displaystyle dT_{t} = ( C T + R ​ T t + F 1 ​ h t + b 2 ​ T t 2 + b 3 ​ T t 3 ) ​ d ​ t + σ T ​ d ​ W t T , \displaystyle=\left(C_{T}+RT_{t}+F_{1}h_{t}+b_{2}T_{t}^{2}+b_{3}T_{t}^{3}\right)dt+\sigma_{T}dW_{t}^{T}, (30) d ​ h t \displaystyle dh_{t} = ( − ϵ ​ h t − F 2 ​ T t ) ​ d ​ t + σ h ​ d ​ W t h . \displaystyle=\left(-\epsilon h_{t}-F_{2}T_{t}\right)dt+\sigma_{h}dW_{t}^{h}. The four linear terms form the oscillatory skeleton of the RO model. With R < 0 R<0 , R ​ T t RT_{t} represents net linear damping of SST anomalies, weakening both warm and cold anomalies. The F 1 ​ h t F_{1}h_{t} term represents delayed oceanic feedback: positive h t h_{t} promotes SST warming, while negative h t h_{t} favors cooling [ 49 ] . The − ϵ ​ h t -\epsilon h_{t} term relaxes the recharge anomaly toward zero, while − F 2 ​ T t -F_{2}T_{t} represents discharge during El Niño and recharge during La Niña, contributing to subsequent phase transitions [ 50 , 11 ] . The quadratic term b 2 ​ T t 2 b_{2}T_{t}^{2} accounts for nonlinear feedbacks that generate warm-cold asymmetry of SST anomalies, including stronger deep atmospheric convection during El Niño, nonlinear dynamical heating [ 51 ] , and thermocline-feedback nonlinearity [ 11 ] . With b 2 > 0 b_{2}>0 , the quadratic term breaks warm-cold symmetry by adding a warming tendency for both positive and negative SST anomalies. The cubic term with b 3 < 0 b_{3}<0 provides nonlinear saturation at large amplitudes. The constant drift C T C_{T} is chosen to offset the nonzero mean induced by the nonlinear feedbacks and maintain the zero-mean SST-anomaly convention. The independent additive noise terms σ T ​ d ​ W t T \sigma_{T}\,dW_{t}^{T} and σ h ​ d ​ W t h \sigma_{h}\,dW_{t}^{h} represent unresolved fast forcing, including short-term wind-stress and heat-flux perturbations [ 11 ] . The second model represents linear drift with multiplicative noise. It retains the linear recharge-discharge skeleton and introduces state-dependent noise in the SST equation: d ​ T t \displaystyle dT_{t} = ( R ​ T t + F 1 ​ h t ) ​ d ​ t + σ T ​ ( T t ) ​ d ​ W t T , \displaystyle=(RT_{t}+F_{1}h_{t})dt+\sigma_{T}(T_{t})dW_{t}^{T}, (31) d ​ h t \displaystyle dh_{t} = ( − ϵ ​ h t − F 2 ​ T t ) ​ d ​ t + σ h ​ d ​ W t h , \displaystyle=(-\epsilon h_{t}-F_{2}T_{t})dt+\sigma_{h}dW_{t}^{h}, where σ T ​ ( T ) = σ 0 ​ ( 1 + B ​ max ⁡ ( T , 0 ) ) . \sigma_{T}(T)=\sigma_{0}\left(1+B\max(T,0)\right). The state-dependent multiplicative noise σ T ​ ( T t ) ​ d ​ W t T \sigma_{T}(T_{t})dW_{t}^{T} accounts for fast atmospheric forcing associated with westerly wind bursts, where brief episodes of anomalous westerly winds can last days up to weeks [ 52 ] . These atmospheric-wind feedbacks tend to be more frequent and stronger during El Niño, strengthening stochastic forcing and contributing to warm-cold asymmetry [ 11 ] . Here, σ 0 \sigma_{0} sets the baseline SST-noise amplitude for T t ≤ 0 T_{t}\leq 0 , while B > 0 B>0 controls the warm-state enhancement of the noise amplitude.

sections.heading: 4.3 Regime switching: deterministic bistability versus hidden double-well forcing
sections.text: We finally consider regime-switching systems, in which the observed variable remains near one of two persistent states for extended periods and occasionally transitions between them [ 54 ] . Such switching can arise through two distinct mechanisms: intrinsic bistability, in which the nonlinear dynamics of the observed variable X t X_{t} itself form a double well and the hidden stochastic forcing Y t Y_{t} can trigger transitions of X t X_{t} between the two wells [ 12 ] , or hidden double-well forcing, in which the dynamics of X t X_{t} are linear and the double-well structure resides in the hidden forcing instead. The deterministic-bistability model places the double-well structure in the deterministic dynamics of the observed variable: d ​ X t \displaystyle dX_{t} = ( a ​ X t − ρ ​ X t 3 + Y t ) ​ d ​ t + σ X ​ d ​ W t X , \displaystyle=(aX_{t}-\rho X_{t}^{3}+Y_{t})dt+\sigma_{X}dW_{t}^{X}, (32) d ​ Y t \displaystyle dY_{t} = − b ​ Y t ​ d ​ t + σ Y ​ d ​ W t Y . \displaystyle=-bY_{t}\,dt+\sigma_{Y}dW_{t}^{Y}. When Y t = 0 Y_{t}=0 , the drift a ​ X t − ρ ​ X t 3 aX_{t}-\rho X_{t}^{3} has an unstable equilibrium at X = 0 X=0 and two stable equilibria at X = ± a / ρ X=\pm\sqrt{a/\rho} . The hidden OU process Y Y acts as a stochastic forcing: a sufficiently strong fluctuation in Y t Y_{t} can push X t X_{t} across the unstable equilibrium into the opposite basin, where the bistable drift stabilizes X t X_{t} in the new regime. In contrast, the hidden-double-well-forcing model treats Z t Z_{t} as a hidden stochastic forcing with its own double-well dynamics: d ​ X t \displaystyle dX_{t} = ( − α ​ X t + Z t ) ​ d ​ t + σ X ​ d ​ W t X , \displaystyle=(-\alpha X_{t}+Z_{t})dt+\sigma_{X}dW_{t}^{X}, (33) d ​ Z t \displaystyle dZ_{t} = ( a Z ​ Z t − ρ Z ​ Z t 3 ) ​ d ​ t + σ Z ​ d ​ W t Z . \displaystyle=(a_{Z}Z_{t}-\rho_{Z}Z_{t}^{3})dt+\sigma_{Z}dW_{t}^{Z}. For a fixed Z t Z_{t} , the dynamics of X t X_{t} are linear and stable, relaxing toward Z t / α Z_{t}/\alpha with no double-well structure of their own. When Z t Z_{t} switches to the opposite well, its forcing drives X t X_{t} toward the corresponding observed regime. As long as Z t Z_{t} remains in that well, its forcing sustains the new observed regime.

sections.heading: 5 Discussion and Conclusions
sections.text: This work introduces an observation-conditioned, model-informed causal fingerprint framework for diagnosing hidden influence in partially-observed dynamical systems. At each state time, the fingerprint measures how future observations revise the inferred hidden state. Evaluated across different future observation windows, it tracks the temporal reach of that influence, while computed along the trajectory, it shows how the pattern changes from one event or event stage to another. Because the observed trajectory is fixed while hidden-state inference depends on the candidate model, fingerprints provide a direct way to compare competing mechanistic explanations of the same observations. In linear Gaussian systems, the analysis yields an explicit characteristic fingerprint timescale for the temporal reach of hidden causal influence. In Test I, the surrogates reproduce the perfect model’s selected observable summary statistics, but removing feedback-induced state memory or suppressing hidden-noise memory changes the strength and temporal structure of their fingerprints. In Test II, the chosen one-component surrogate reproduces features of the fast marginal fingerprint but misses the slow component’s contribution over longer future observation windows. These tests demonstrate how fingerprint patterns reveal omitted or misrepresented hidden mechanisms. The nonlinear tests demonstrate event-level diagnosis of competing hidden mechanisms. For the observed amplitude burst generated by the multiplicative-instability model, fingerprint responses appear earlier under that model, whereas the additive-forcing model’s responses are more closely aligned with the burst’s growth. In the oscillatory variability case study, distinct responses during La Niña development show how deterministic nonlinear feedback and state-dependent stochastic forcing assign different roles to the hidden recharge state. For regime switching, deterministic-bistability fingerprints respond during transitions and within-regime fluctuations, whereas hidden-double-well-forcing fingerprints are more concentrated near transitions. Across these examples, inference models with similar observable behavior can assign hidden influence to different times and stages of an event. The fingerprint should be interpreted as a model-relative diagnostic rather than a model-free interventional proof of causality. Its mechanistic interpretation depends on the candidate dynamical structure, the chosen hidden-state representation, and the accuracy of the filtering and smoothing distributions. A fingerprint therefore does not by itself establish that one candidate mechanism is the true physical mechanism; instead, it reveals how competing models assign hidden influence to the same observed evolution. In non-Gaussian settings, approximate posterior methods such as the ensemble calculation in Section 4.3 introduce an additional layer of approximation. Future work could extend the framework to higher-dimensional nonlinear systems with multiple interacting hidden and observed variables. A key question is how to resolve the joint and individual contributions of hidden processes to different observed variables and trace these influences over time. Another direction is to apply the framework to real-world observations, extending beyond the present ENSO experiment, which uses observational statistics for parameter selection but model-generated trajectories for causal diagnosis. Fingerprints computed along observed SST-anomaly trajectories could help diagnose how alternative mechanisms explain the evolution of individual El Niño and La Niña events. Such analyses could clarify the roles of different physical processes and inform the construction of conceptual and reduced models.

Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: arXiv.org perpetual non-exclusive license arXiv:2610.22286v1 [math.DS] 15 Oct 2026 Causal Fingerprints Reveal Hidden Mechanisms in Partially-Observed Dynamical Systems Zhang Jiang Marios Andreou Nan Chen † † thanks: Corresponding author: chennan@math.wisc.edu Affiliation: Department of Mathematics, University of Wisconsin–Madison, Madison, WI 53706, USA Abstract In partially-observed dynamical systems, distinct hidden mechanisms can produce similar observable summary statistics while explaining individual events differently. Matching statistics therefore does not guarantee matching mechanisms. We introduce causal fingerprints: realization-dependent patterns that track how information about a hidden state is revealed through subsequent evolution. Within a prescribed dynamical model, we compare the filtering posterior, based on observations up to a given time, with the smoothing posterior, obtained after adding an expanding window of future observations. We quantify this retrospective information gain using Kullback-Leibler divergence and track its evolution as the future window of observational data expands. The fingerprint reveals both the strength and temporal reach of hidden influence, which can vary across events and their stages. Because the observed trajectory is held fixed while hidden-state inference depends on the candidate model, fingerprints reveal how competing dynamical mechanisms explain the same observations even when selected statistics agree. In linear Gaussian systems, we derive a characteristic fingerprint timescale for the temporal reach of hidden influence. Calibrated surrogates matching the observable mean, variance, and decorrelation time can still produce distinct fingerprints when feedback memory, hidden-noise memory, or hidden forcing timescales are misrepresented. Nonlinear examples reveal mechanism-dependent signatures for extreme bursts, oscillatory variability, and regime switching, including multiplicative instability versus additive forcing, deterministic nonlinear feedback versus state-dependent multiplicative noise, and intrinsic bistability versus hidden double-well forcing. Causal fingerprints therefore provide a time- and event-resolved diagnostic for asking not only whether a model reproduces observed statistics, but how its hidden dynamics explain individual events. Models with distinct mechanisms can reproduce similar statistical patterns yet explain the same observed event differently. Telling these mechanistic explanations apart is particularly difficult when the variables that drive an event are hidden from observation. However, a hidden variable that drives the later evolution of the observed variables leaves information in subsequent observations, so these observations can refine the inference about the earlier state of the hidden variable. We quantify this information gain as causal fingerprints, which reveal how strongly hidden variables influence the observed evolution and how long this influence persists across the stages of individual events. In examples involving extreme bursts, oscillatory variability, and regime switching, models with closely matched statistics produce distinct fingerprints along the same observed trajectories, showing that fingerprints reveal the different mechanisms through which these models explain each event. 1 Introduction Complex dynamical systems arise throughout science and engineering, including geophysical dynamics [ 1 ] , turbulence [ 2 ] , neuroscience [ 3 ] , epidemiology [ 4 ] , and financial markets [ 5 ] . A defining feature of many such systems is that they are partially observed: in practice, the observed variables represent only a subset of the full dynamical state, while many relevant variables remain hidden or unresolved due to limited observations, coarse-grained modeling, or intrinsic spatiotemporal multiscale structures [ 6 ] . These hidden variables often represent slow environmental drivers, unresolved sub-grid or small-scale processes [ 2 ] , or latent regulatory mechanisms [ 3 ] . A central challenge in studying partially-observed systems is that different hidden mechanisms can produce very similar observable statistics, such as probability distributions, autocorrelations, or energy spectra [ 7 , 8 ] . As a result, model identification based solely on observable statistics can admit different explanations for the underlying latent dynamics [ 9 ] . Understanding the causal influence that hidden variables have on the observables’ evolution is therefore essential, providing insight into the mechanisms that drive observable variability and shape phenomena such as extreme events [ 10 ] , oscillatory variability [ 11 ] , and regime transitions [ 12 ] . In dynamical systems, such influence can vary substantially along a trajectory and across different stages of an event, making time-local and event-resolved diagnosis particularly important. Existing causal inference frameworks have been successfully applied to a wide range of dynamical systems. Methods such as Granger causality [ 13 ] , transfer entropy [ 14 ] , and graphical-model-based approaches [ 15 ] are particularly useful for identifying statistical or predictive relationships among observed, or reliably reconstructed, variables. However, their considered setting poses two significant difficulties. First, some of the variables responsible for the observed evolution are themselves hidden. Second, their influence may change substantially along a trajectory, so relationships inferred from long records can miss mechanisms that become important only during a particular event or stage of an event. Our interest is therefore not only in whether a causal relationship exists on average, but in how hidden influence unfolds during an individual realization. A complementary line of work uses dynamical structures more explicitly. Information-flow formulations [ 16 ] , perturbation experiments [ 17 ] , and response-theory approaches [ 18 ] , including fluctuation-dissipation methods, use the governing dynamics to characterize directional entropy transfer, sensitivity, or response to perturbations. The question considered here is different: an observed trajectory is given while important causal variables remain hidden, with candidate models providing competing explanations for the latent dynamics behind that trajectory. This motivates the concept of causal fingerprints for partially-observed dynamical systems. Distinct latent mechanisms can produce similar observable statistics, making them difficult to distinguish using probability distributions, long-time correlations, or related diagnostics [ 19 , 7 ] . Yet they need not explain an individual trajectory in the same way. Hidden influence may become important at different stages of an event or remain relevant over different future horizons. We refer to these realization-dependent temporal patterns of hidden-to-observed influence as causal fingerprints. Building on assimilative causal inference and related work on causal influence ranges [ 10 , 20 ] , we use these realization-dependent fingerprints to diagnose competing dynamical mechanisms. Fingerprints computed under different candidate models can be compared along the same observed trajectory, revealing differences in the hidden dynamical explanations assigned to the observations. To quantify these patterns, we adopt a Bayesian inverse-problem perspective of causality [ 10 ] . When a hidden state affects the subsequent observed evolution, later observations can sharpen the inference of that earlier state. Using data assimilation [ 21 , 22 ] , we compare the filtering posterior based on observations up to the current time with the smoothing posterior obtained after incorporating an expanding window of future observations [ 23 ] . Extending this future window tracks how far information about the hidden state persists in the subsequent observations. Repeating the comparison along the trajectory shows how this pattern changes across events and during their various stages of onset, development, peak, and decay.
